newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Tokyo stocks tumble, Taipei bourse sharply up.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo stocks tumble, Taipei bourse sharply up.

text.p: Fading interest in blue chips sent Tokyo's stock market tumbling through the 21,000 level on Monday but in Taipei late buying pushed the index up more than two percent to a 22-month high.
In Hong Kong, the key Hang Seng index finished up almost one percent. Bombay's bourse was the biggest Asian loser outside Tokyo, shedding 1.34 percent.

Brokers said Tokyo's key Nikkei 225 average fell 1.64 percent after a recent boom in blue-chip issues waned, triggering a wave of selling at the end of an otherwise dull session. The Nikkei ended at 20,674.69, down 345.67 points.
The fading interest in big-name global shares pulled away one of the main market props and the fall was accentuated by thin volume.
The Nikkei average is likely to gauge the bottom of the recent range this week, after it tested the upper side last week," said Tetsuya Ishijima, chief strategist at Okasan Securities Co Ltd.
"The focus is on whether it will be supported at around 20,500," he said.
Hong Kong stocks ended sharply higher as a decline in the U.S. long bond yield gave prices a lift and market optimism kept selling interest at a minimum, traders said.
The Hang Seng index finished up 123.63 points, or 0.92 percent, at 13,517.56, its session high.
"People who are long and overweight in the market, they don't see any major bad news on the horizon to sell stocks," said analyst Paul Chan of Merrill Lynch Asset Management.
Others said market participants were also reacting to movement in the bond market and while there were still buyers around, few were keen to sell.
On Friday, the U.S. long bond rose 31/32, bringing the yield down to 6.36 percent, its lowest level since March 4.
Strong late buying in profit-backed plastics pulled Taiwan's stock index to a sharply higher close, up 156.75 points or 2.30 percent to end at 6,982.81.

Brokers said late buying focused on stocks related to the Formosa group, one of Taiwan's biggest and most influential conglomerates, driving the market to a 22-month closing high. The New Zealand share market, encouraged by a strong debt market, staged a surprisingly strong performance, brokers said.
The top 40 index ended 19.47 points or 0.83 percent up at 2,367.89 as indicator 90-day bank bills rallied 17 basis points.
Doyle Paterson Brown broker Philip Solarz said the uncertain political situation, with no government formed since the October 12 election, did not appear to be deterring investors.
Parliament must meet by December 13 and talks on forming a coalition with the NZ First party continued on Monday.
Bombay shares erased early morning gains to end sharply down as negative sentiment prevailed, traders said.
"It was a pretty bad day. Overall, sentiment continues to be bearish," said Dheeraj Agarwal, trader at SS Kantilal Ishwarlal Securities, a local brokerage.
Dealers said new rules on short selling announced by market regulator the Securities & Exchange Board of India (SEBI) limited trading volumes and kept major players to the sidelines.
The benchmark Bombay Stock Exchange's (BSE) top index fell 38.65 points to end at a provisional 2,851.85.
Thai stocks closed lower in thin trade after investors sold across the board on continued concerns over Thailand's slow economic growth and lagging exports, brokers said.
The SET index, which moved sluggishly throughout the session, dropped for the third consecutive trading day, falling 5.34 points or 0.58 percent to 920.63.
SIMEX Brent crude futures in Asia were traded firmer.
January Brent was traded at $22.85, up from its last London settlement of $22.77.
At 1147 GMT the dollar traded at 113.68/3.78 yen and 1.5415/18 marks.
